dataset.input: The National Assembly wishes to amend the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999 to alter the procedure for amending the Constitution itself. The bill proposes that future amendments require only a simple majority vote in each chamber. The bill passes both the Senate and House of Representatives with a two-thirds majority and is transmitted to the state Houses of Assembly. Is this procedure valid?
dataset.target: No. Section 9 of the Constitution prescribes the procedure for amendments. Section 9(1)-(2) requires a bill passed by a two-thirds majority of each chamber of the National Assembly and approved by a resolution of at least two-thirds of the state Houses of Assembly (24 out of 36 states). However, the Constitution does not specifically provide an 'entrenched' or 'double entrenchment' mechanism that would make the amendment procedure itself immune from simpler amendment. The amendment procedure can itself be amended using the same procedure required for ordinary amendments (two-thirds of National Assembly + two-thirds of states). However, introducing a simple majority requirement would still require the existing two-thirds procedure to be followed first. If all procedural requirements were met, including state assembly approval, the change would be effective, though it would be a matter of significant constitutional controversy.
dataset.source: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, s. 9

dataset.input: A bill to alter the Constitution to create new states passes the Senate with 70 of 109 senators voting in favour and passes the House of Representatives with 280 of 360 members voting in favour. The bill is then sent to the state Houses of Assembly. Only 20 state Houses of Assembly approve the bill. Has the bill been validly passed?
dataset.target: No. Section 9(2) of the Constitution requires that the bill be approved by a resolution of at least two-thirds of all state Houses of Assembly (24 out of 36 states). Since only 20 states approved, this falls short of the required 24. The bill has not been validly passed. Additionally, the creation of new states is governed by section 8, which requires additional conditions including: (a) a request supported by at least a two-thirds majority of members of the legislative houses in the area demanding the creation; (b) approval in a referendum by at least a two-thirds majority of the people in the area; and (c) approval by a simple majority of all states of the Federation. Both section 8 and section 9 requirements must be satisfied for a valid creation of new states.
dataset.source: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, ss. 8, 9

dataset.input: The National Assembly passes an Act regulating the procedure for the impeachment of the President, going beyond what is stated in the Constitution. The Act introduces additional procedural requirements not found in section 143 of the Constitution. The President challenges the Act as unconstitutional. Is the Act valid?
dataset.target: No. The Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation, and any law inconsistent with its provisions is void to the extent of the inconsistency (section 1(3)). Section 143 comprehensively sets out the procedure for the impeachment of the President, and the National Assembly cannot add to or alter this procedure by ordinary legislation. The National Assembly would need to amend the Constitution itself (pursuant to section 9) to change the impeachment procedure. The Supreme Court has held that where the Constitution exhaustively provides for a procedure, the National Assembly cannot introduce additional requirements by ordinary legislation. The Act is void for inconsistency with section 143 and section 1(3) of the Constitution.
dataset.source: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, ss. 1(3), 143
